newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ June qtr GDP unlikely to surprise - economists.
newsitem.headline: NZ June qtr GDP unlikely to surprise - economists.

text.p: Market reaction to New Zealand June quarter GDP figures due on Friday is expected to be muted, with any potential for a rally on the back of a weak number curbed by strong wage data released on Tuesday.

Bain and Co economist Ulf Schoefisch told Reuters he expected no market reaction at all if June quarter seasonally adjusted production-based GDP fell between 0.4 and 0.6 percent. Bain and Co is picking 0.5 percent.
March quarter data showed a 0.4 percent rise.

Schoefisch said while a surprisingly weak June quarter number might provide an offset to strong employment data released today, it would not prompt the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) to revise its forecasts.
"If it's a tick lower for the bank they will obviously like that, but it won't have any consequences for monetary policy."

Asked if there was any chance of a market-led easing on the back of a weak GDP number, Schoefisch replied: "No, I wouldn't think so, not after today's number. Today's number was a very, very bad number and will completely override any positive news that is going to come for a while."
Statistics New Zealand said earlier that average hourly earnings rose 3.3 percent in the May year, with private sector earnings rising four percent.

Westpac Economist Hamish Macalister, who is picking 0.1 percent June quarter GDP growth for a 1.4 percent annual rise, said Westpac expects annual averages to show a general slowing in the economy's rate of growth, before it begins to pick up again in the first half of 1997.
He said Friday's release was likely to contain few surprises and would not have any implications for the RBNZ.
"We realise that we're at the bottom end...of expectations but we certainly don't expect to see anything below that. The possible risk there is on the upside rather than the downside," he added.

Jason Wong, economist at First NZ Capital, said recent data suggested June quarter GDP would be at least as strong as the March quarter, and he expected a 0.6 percent rise. He said a strong growth figure would prompt little market reaction, but people might extend their forecasts for when an easing in monetary conditions was likely.

The economists said September quarter GDP data would be the first to show the impact of the government's NZ$3.1 billion two-year tax cut and social spending package, the first round of which was implemented on July 1.
"The feeling across the market seems to be that really the impact of the tax cuts is going to be a lot less than people had initially anticipated," Macalister said.

"Although we haven't had too much data yet to confirm this picture, we suspect that in fact a lot of the impact of the tax cut was felt in the economy before they actually came into place. You had a lot of retailers offering discounts, you know,
"don't pay till after the tax cuts", and so on," he said.
Schoefisch said the effect of consumer spending in anticipation of the tax cuts was not very strong.
